title: Prefix Common Array of Two Permutations
description:
# Prefix Common Array of Two Permutations

You are given two permutations `A` and `B` of the numbers from `1` to `n`.

For each index `i`, compare the prefixes `A[0..i]` and `B[0..i]`. Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the number of distinct values that appear in both prefixes.

Because `A` and `B` are permutations, each value appears exactly once in each array.

## Example 1

**Input**
A = [1,3,2,4], B = [3,1,2,4]

**Output**
[0,2,3,4]

**Explanation**
At `i = 0`, prefixes are `[1]` and `[3]`, so there are no common values.
At `i = 1`, prefixes are `[1,3]` and `[3,1]`, so values `1` and `3` are common.
At `i = 2`, value `2` is also common.
At `i = 3`, all four values are common.

## Example 2

**Input**
A = [2,3,1], B = [3,1,2]

**Output**
[0,1,3]

## Constraints

* `1 <= A.length == B.length <= 100000`
* `A` and `B` are permutations of the integers from `1` to `n`.

solutions.name: Shared Occurrence Counter
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use one integer array `seen` for both permutations. At index `i`, increment the counter for `A[i]` and the counter for `B[i]`. When a counter becomes `2`, that value has now appeared in both prefixes.

## Key Insight
Since both arrays are permutations, a value can be seen at most once from `A` and once from `B`. Therefore the exact moment its shared counter reaches `2` is the first prefix where it should contribute to the answer.

## Complexity Analysis
Each index performs constant work, so the time complexity is O(n). The counter array has length `n + 1`, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Two Seen Arrays
solutions.description:
## Approach
Maintain `seenA` and `seenB` separately. After adding `A[i]` to the first prefix and `B[i]` to the second prefix, check whether the newly added values are already present on the opposite side.

## Key Insight
Only the two newly added values can change the answer at step `i`. If `A[i]` was already in `B`'s prefix, it becomes newly common; if `B[i]` was already in `A`'s prefix, it also becomes newly common. When the two values are equal, count it only once.

## Complexity Analysis
Every index is processed once, so the time complexity is O(n). The two boolean arrays store whether each value has appeared in each prefix, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Set Intersection Per Prefix
solutions.description:
## Approach
Maintain the two prefix sets explicitly. After each index, count how many values from the first prefix set are also present in the second prefix set.

## Key Insight
This route follows the definition directly: `answer[i]` is the size of the intersection of the two prefix sets. It is slower, but it is useful as a correctness baseline.

## Complexity Analysis
At step `i`, scanning the first prefix set can cost O(i), so the total time complexity is O(n^2). The two sets store up to `n` values, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Fenwick Tree On B Positions
solutions.description:
## Approach
Precompute the position of every value in `B`. While scanning `A`, add the position of `A[i]` in `B` to a Fenwick tree. Then `answer[i]` is how many added positions are at most `i`.

## Key Insight
A value from the prefix of `A` is also in the prefix of `B[0..i]` exactly when its position in `B` is at most `i`. This turns prefix common counting into prefix sum queries over positions.

## Complexity Analysis
Each update and prefix query costs O(log n), so the total time complexity is O(n log n). The position array, answer array, and Fenwick tree all use O(n) space.
